name: Macassar oil

card.summary: The Victorian hair oil that gave us the antimacassar; historically marketed for growth and styling, with no clinical evidence behind the growth claims.
card.note: Historical product; regrowth claims were advertising claims and have not been studied.

quick.overview:
Macassar oil was a perfumed vegetable-based hair oil popular with men in the 1800s. Alexander Rowland sold it from about 1793 and advertised it widely.

Its grease on chair backs gave rise to the antimacassar cloth.
quick.mechanism: It was a plain emollient hair dressing that coated and smoothed hair; advertised effects on growth have not been studied.
quick.risks: No specific harms are documented in the available sources. Its main historical drawback was staining of upholstery.

lead: Macassar oil was a scented compound hair oil used mainly by men in Western Europe in the 19th and early 20th centuries to condition, smooth and style hair into a glossy, controlled look. Applied generously, it gave the sleek, parted hairstyles of the Victorian and Edwardian eras their shine and hold, and it replaced earlier dressings such as bear's grease with a perfumed alternative.[1][2]

It was popularised by the London barber Alexander Rowland (1747-1823), who from about 1793 sold Rowland's Macassar Oil; within roughly two decades it was heavily advertised, making it one of the first nationally advertised products.[1] Advertisements made broad claims, including that it would regrow hair for balding men, a claim lampooned in a c. 1814 Thomas Rowlandson illustration.[1]

Its name refers to the port of Makassar in Sulawesi, where ingredients were reputedly bought.[1] The oil was greasy enough to stain upholstery, which led to the antimacassar, a washable cloth protecting chair backs.[1] Lord Byron mocked "thine incomparable oil, Macassar" in Don Juan, and Lewis Carroll mentions it in Through the Looking-Glass.[1]

Hair conditioned, slicked and held in place
angle.text: Men applied the oil to smooth and condition hair and hold sleek styles with a high shine. Advertisements also promised hair growth, a claim that has not been studied.

infobox: Schleichera oleosa (kusum) oil, later coconut or palm oil, ylang-ylang scent[1][2]

paras: Wikipedia reports the oil was first made from the oil of Macassar ebony or Schleichera oleosa, called kayu hitam in Indonesia, where it is still used; as the tree became scarce through overharvesting for timber, makers shifted to vegetable oils such as coconut, palm or kusum, often blended with ylang-ylang for fragrance.[1] Grokipedia gives a similar account, adding that alcohol and castor oil were used in some formulations to thin the mix.[2]

Rowland began selling the oil around 1793, and the family firm A. Rowland & Sons registered the name as a trademark in 1888.[1] Wikipedia notes that Rowland's son later credited a relative on Celebes with helping source the base ingredient.[1] Advertising claimed regrowth for balding men; a c. 1814 Thomas Rowlandson illustration satirised such claims, and Lord Byron and Lewis Carroll referred to the oil in their writing.[1]

Because the oil rubbed off onto furniture, the antimacassar, a small crocheted, embroidered or mass-produced cloth, was placed on chair backs to protect upholstery.[1] Alternatives such as brilliantine, pomade and Brylcreem later became common.[1]
No studies found. A 1998 patent application describes a method of extracting Macassar oil from Schleichera trijuga seeds for use as a cosmetic hair and scalp agent, but it is not a clinical study.[3]
